title: The one tie between two groups
hook: News from another friend group has one way in. What kind of tie is it?

knows: what a link between two people means
doesNotKnow: that if you are close to two people, strong triadic closure makes them know each other, so the only link between two groups cannot be a close one

misconception: News and job leads reach you through your closest friends, so the closer the tie, the more it brings you.
objective: The learner can explain that when A is close to B and to a groupmate C, the rule needs a B–C link that does not exist, so the only link between two groups whose members have close friends inside must be an acquaintance, and news from outside the group crosses it.

claims.text: Rule used in the lesson (strong triadic closure): if a person is close to two people, those two have a tie (close or acquaintance). Stage: "Rule: two people you’re close to must have a tie." Question: "Every tie is close or an acquaintance."
claims.source: Easley & Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 §3.1 (section number unconfirmed), strong triadic closure property. A rule of this lesson, not an empirical law. | v2 (2026-10-14): stage and question wording changed ("linked" -> "have a tie"; the two kinds of tie named); earlier fact-check (pass NCM-1) applied to the v1 wording. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. Stage line 'Rule: two people you're close to must have a tie.' and question 'Every tie is close or an acquaintance.' match the claim text; it is the strong triadic closure property of Easley and Kleinberg ch. 3 (section unconfirmed), stated as the lesson's rule.

claims.text: In the stage graph (two groups of four, every pair inside a group linked, plus the one link A–B; 13 links), A–B is the only link whose ends share no neighbour (the only local bridge), and with A–B close the rule breaks: B and C are both close to A but are not linked.
claims.source: Node enumeration (builder, 2026-10-14; same rule as the code): local bridges = [A-B]. With all 12 in-group links close and A–B close there are 6 broken triples (A: C-B, D-B, E-B; B: F-A, G-A, H-A); the stage draws one (C–B). With A–B an acquaintance, 0 broken. C–E and F–H exist (the two check triangles). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Own enumeration (fc/news.mjs): 13 links; local bridges = [A-B]; all-close gives 6 broken triples (A: CB, DB, EB; B: FA, GA, HA); A-B weak gives 0; B-C absent; C-E and F-H present.

claims.text: The same break hits D and E, and on B’s side F, G and H. So while A or B has a close friend in their own group, the one tie between the groups must be an acquaintance.
claims.source: Node enumeration of all 2^13 = 8,192 close/acquaintance labellings of the 13 links: 4,160 satisfy the rule; 64 make A–B close, and in all 64 neither A nor B has another close tie (0 exceptions). General form: Easley & Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3 §3.2 (section number unconfirmed): under strong triadic closure, a node with at least two strong ties cannot have a strong local bridge. Counts are evidence only, not learner text. | v2 (2026-10-14): learner text reworded; "the same break" = the 6 broken triples of c2 (A: C-B, D-B, E-B; B: F-A, G-A, H-A), re-run in node. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. Own enumeration of all 2^13 labellings of the 13 links: 4,160 satisfy the rule; 64 have A-B close, with 0 exceptions (in all 64 neither A nor B has a close tie in its group). With every inside tie close the broken triples are exactly A: C-B, D-B, E-B and B: F-A, G-A, H-A, which is 'the same break hits D and E, and on B's side F, G and H'.

claims.text: News from outside your group comes in over that tie (in this model: on the stage, news from H reaches A’s group only across A–B, shown as an acquaintance).
claims.source: Follows from c2 and c3: A–B is the only link between the groups, and it must be an acquaintance. The stage sends news H → F, G, B → A → C, D, E. | v2 (2026-10-14): reworded; the hook no longer says acquaintances bring the most news, only that news from another group has one way in. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-2): VERIFIED. A-B is the only link between the groups (edge list), so news from H reaches A, C, D, E only across it (HOP map H -> F, G, B -> A -> C, D, E). The reveal's 'you saw it reach A's group across the acquaintance A-B' is gated by the 'news-over-weak' milestone (only fires with A-B an acquaintance).

claims.text: NOT IN LEARNER TEXT. Granovetter (1973): of people who found a job through a contact, 16.7% saw the contact often, 55.6% occasionally, 27.8% rarely.
claims.source: Granovetter, M. S. (1973), "The Strength of Weak Ties", American Journal of Sociology 78(6), as reported in Easley & Kleinberg (2010) ch. 3. Empirical: needs a human source check by the fact-checker (the brief's author could not open the paper). 9, 30 and 15 of 54 reproduce the percentages to 0.1 (node). Kept out of the hook, stage and reveal until checked. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass NCM-1): Not in learner text. Primary paper (AJS 78(6)) unreachable through the proxy. Secondary sources via search (Wikipedia "Interpersonal ties": 16.7/55.6/27.8%, N = 54, often = at least twice a week, occasionally, rarely = once a year or less) agree, and 9/30/15 of 54 reproduce them, but per the pass brief a figure not confirmed from the cited source is not verified. Before any learner use: a human checks Granovetter 1973, p. 1371.

recall.question: Two friend groups are joined by a single link, Sam–Lee. Sam has close friends in his group, and close friends of one person always know each other. What can the Sam–Lee link be?
recall.why: If Sam were close to Lee and to a groupmate, that groupmate and Lee would have to be linked, but Sam–Lee is the only link between the groups. So it must be an acquaintance.
